lessons.title: Leadership and how teams develop
lessons.html:
Leading versus managing

Managing is about planning, organising and controlling work: rosters, feed sheets, records. Leading is about influencing people so they want to do the work well. A dairy team leader needs both. You can roster a milker for 04:00, but whether that milker follows the full routine when nobody is watching depends on leadership.

Leadership styles

StyleDescriptionWhen it works
Directive (autocratic)Leader decides and gives instructionsEmergencies, safety issues, new and inexperienced workers
Participative (democratic)Leader involves the team in decisionsImproving routines, solving recurring problems, experienced teams
DelegatingLeader gives responsibility to capable team membersSkilled, reliable workers who can run a task on their own
CoachingLeader teaches and supports while guidingWorkers who are keen but still learning

Situational leadership means choosing the style that fits the person and the task, rather than using one style for everything.

Stages of team development

A common model describes teams moving through stages:

  1. Forming: members are new, polite, unsure of roles.
  2. Storming: disagreements about roles, shifts and ways of working.
  3. Norming: the team agrees how things are done.
  4. Performing: the team works well with little supervision.

New staff or a change in leader can send a team back to an earlier stage. Expect it and guide the team through it with clear roles and fair handling of conflict.

Qualities of a good team leader

  • Fair and consistent with everyone.
  • Leads by example: punctual, wears protective equipment, follows the routine.
  • Communicates clearly and listens.
  • Knows the work well enough to teach it.
  • Takes responsibility instead of blaming.

lessons.title: Motivation, communication and delegation
lessons.html:
What motivates people

Maslow's hierarchy of needs suggests people are first motivated by basic needs (pay, food, housing), then safety (safe work, job security), then belonging (being part of a team), then esteem (recognition, respect) and finally self-actualisation (growth, reaching potential). Herzberg described hygiene factors, such as pay, conditions and supervision, which cause dissatisfaction if poor, and motivators, such as achievement, recognition and responsibility, which drive real commitment.

On a dairy, this means: fix basic problems first (fair pay, safe equipment, decent conditions), then build motivation with recognition, responsibility and development.

Effective communication

  • Clear message: what, why, how, by when.
  • Right channel: face to face for important or sensitive matters; boards and written notes for routine information.
  • Language: use the language the team understands best; check understanding.
  • Two-way: ask for questions and ideas, and actually listen.
  • Non-verbal: tone and body language must match the message.

Giving feedback

A useful structure is: describe the behaviour, explain its effect, and agree on what should happen next. Example: "Yesterday the post-dip was skipped on row two. Those cows are now at higher risk of mastitis. From today, please dip every cow, and tell me if the dip cup is not working." Praise in public; correct in private.

Delegation

  1. Choose the right person for the task.
  2. Explain the result needed, the standard and the deadline.
  3. Give the authority and resources to do it.
  4. Agree on check-in points.
  5. Follow up and give recognition.

You can delegate tasks and authority, but you remain accountable for the result.

lessons.title: Conflict, problem solving and team performance
lessons.html:
Handling conflict

Conflict is normal in teams that work long shifts together. Common causes on dairies are unfair rosters, overtime, unclear roles, personality clashes and cultural misunderstandings. Unresolved conflict lowers performance and can turn into grievances or disputes.

Approaches to conflict

  • Avoiding: ignoring it. Only suitable for trivial issues.
  • Accommodating: giving in to keep peace.
  • Competing: one side wins. Needed for safety rules that are not negotiable.
  • Compromising: each side gives something.
  • Collaborating: working together for a solution that meets both sides' needs. Usually best for lasting problems.

Steps: meet the parties, listen to each side, focus on the issue not the person, look for options, agree on a solution, record and follow up. Use the farm's grievance procedure when needed. Labour law, including the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995, protects workers' rights to raise grievances.

Problem solving

  1. Define the problem with facts: "Calf deaths rose from 2 to 7 this month."
  2. Find root causes: ask why repeatedly. Why did calves die? Scours. Why? Late colostrum. Why? The night calving check was skipped. Why? No one was rostered after a staff change.
  3. Generate solutions with the team.
  4. Choose and implement, with responsibilities and dates.
  5. Check the result.

Team performance

Set clear, measurable goals, such as SCC below the buyer's bonus level, calf mortality targets or milking routine compliance. Share results regularly, celebrate progress and address under-performance early with coaching before discipline.

Diversity and respect

Dairy teams often include different languages, cultures, ages and genders. Treat everyone with equal respect; unfair discrimination is prohibited by the Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998.

Key points

  • Use the leadership style that fits the person and the task.
  • Teams pass through forming, storming, norming and performing.
  • Fix hygiene factors, then motivate with recognition and responsibility.
  • Delegate tasks but stay accountable.
  • Handle conflict early and solve problems by finding root causes.
